newsitem.title: CUBA: Dollar fall against "mighty" peso cheers Cubans.
newsitem.headline: Dollar fall against "mighty" peso cheers Cubans.

text.p: Although the Cuban peso is so puny that it is not even a convertible currency on the world market, within this socialist island it has been flexing its muscles on the money exchange to the relief of Fidel Castro's economic strategists.

Juventud Rebelde reported on Sunday that 22 Cuban pesos can now buy a dollar, the lowest official exhange rate since the government legalized the possession and use of foreign currency by Cubans in August 1993.
The news was welcomed by Cubans who get paid in the local currency but yearn for the "verde" (greenbacks) that can be used at special dollar stores to buy products unavailable in Cuban peso shops.
The dollars can be bought at CADECA currency exchange bureaux which were established last year. There are now 24 bureaux with plans to open another 14.

Prior to CADECA, there was a thriving black market currency exchange for those Cubans who could afford to buy them. Between 1991 and 1995 the prices for a single dollar on the black market varied between 80 and 150 pesos. The average wage in Cuba is about 250 pesos a month.
CADECA, which was the brainchild of Cuba's new generation of economists, confounded pundits by forcing the value of the dollar down after it entered the money market.

Juventud Rebelde said that the new strength of the pesos is, in part, based on the greater availability of foods and services paid for in pesos over the past year. With more goods available to buy with pesos, there has been less demand for dollars and so their value has fallen.
This greater availability of goods was due to an increase in production which reached a critically low stage after the fall of Cuba's benefactor, the Soviet Union, in 1991.

Cuban officials have said that absenteeism had dropped off considerably since the buying power of the pesos had increased. Private enterprise food markets, which were legalized in September 1994, are stocked with a wide variety of produce, including pork. With prices bases on supply and demand, they deal only in pesos and have been doing a thriving business.

At the same time, the drop in the price of the dollar on the money exchange now makes it possible for many Cuban families to acquire some dollars to buy basic products that still cannot be found in the government's peso stores.

At present, many families with an income of 280 pesos a month, on the medium range of the pay scale, can afford to exchange 80 pesos for 4 dollars which will buy them a liter (quart) of vegetable oil, a kilogram (2 pounds) of flour and several bars of soap, all in short supply in the peso stores.
Juventud Rebelde quoted Manuel Vale, president of CADECA, as saying that he foresees a further fall in the strengh of the dollar but could not forecast when.
